Q: Initializing python dataclass object without passing instance variables or default values A:

You could add the attribute post-creation:

@dataclass
class TestClass:
  paramA: str
  paramB: float

obj1 = TestClass(paramA = "something", paramB = 123)
obj1.paramC = "New string"

Q: Java 17 for Hadoop and Java 24 A:

Windows can have as many Java's installed as you need without conflicting with others.

After you install Hadoop on Windows, you need to set your environment variables with the HADOOP_HOME and HADOOP_CONF_DIR.

The config directory will contain hadoop-env.cmd. In that file, you can override set JAVA_HOME=%JAVA_HOME% with the path to your Java 17 installation path, then HDFS, YARN, and MapReduce will all use that path. If you install additional tools, such as Hive/Spark/Flink, then you similarly will have to update their configs.

For any Java development, you will still need to configure Maven/Gradle to compile to Java 17.

Q: Is there a way to make scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') accurate? A:

What seems to be happening is that if your initial guess has more than 8 digits correct then the evaluation of cos(x) at double precision already satisfies the minimisation constraint being equal to -1 and so scipi has nothing to do and returns the initial guess. No further improvement is possible. Some optimisers will find the ends of the range of contiguous zeros and return the mid point but evidently scipi doesn't do this.

This is more of a problem with the numerical limitations of evaluating cos(x) near an integer multiple of pi at double precision.

 cos(pi + x) ~= -1 + x^2/2 - O(x^4)

so that when |x| < 1.4e-8 (empirically 1.0395e-8) the answer will be -1.0

If you want the optimiser to be able to solve it then add one to it and use the identity:

 1 + cos(pi + x)  = 2*sin(x/2)^2

These are the plots of both functions - note how heavily quantised cos(pi+x) is! And also that evaluated by math.cos it is zero for a wide range of inputs either side of pi.

Your Newton Raphson method is actually solving the very much easier problem -sin(x) = 0 which is perfectly well behaved.

my_answer = simple_newton_solver_for_comparison(
    f=lambda x:analytic_jac([x])[0],
    df=lambda x:analytic_hess([x])[0][0],
    initial_guess=initial_guess,
  )

Should be instead

my_answer = simple_newton_solver_for_comparison(
    f=lambda x:fun([x])[0],
    df=lambda x:analytic_jac([x])[0],
    initial_guess=initial_guess,
  )

That change should make it do exactly the same as scipi when optimising fun().

If you suspect that an optimiser has not done its job correctly then stepping away from the alleged solution by a factor of (1 + sqrt(machine_eps) will give it a sporting chance of hitting the true minimum.

Q: Type hint a default return type used unless more specific overload exists A:

Your 5 overload method is, as far as I know, the best way to achieve what you want, but if you really want to reduce the amount of overload you need to use at the cost of a potential type inference error. This is a tradeoff you might accept or not. See the answer from sterliakov for more information: https://stackoverflow.com/a/74567241/6251742

Here is an example that works without numpy installed, your IDE should tell you the return type expected for those two calls, and you can replace whatever you need to fit your usecase:

import typing

type T = str | int


@typing.overload
def foo(  # type: ignore[overload-overlap]
    a: str, b: str, c: str, d: str
) -> str: ...


@typing.overload
def foo(a: T, b: T, c: T, d: T) -> int: ...


def foo(a, b, c, d):
    ...


# If all arguments are of type string, then the revealled type will be str
typing.reveal_type(foo("1", "2", "3", "4"))  # str

# If any of those args are of type int, the result will be int
typing.reveal_type(foo("1", "2", "3", 4))  # int

The ignore comment will silence the typechecker warning about overlap. This overlap is intended, and the ignore won't silence anything else and it won't alter the typechecker ability to infer the correct type.

Q: error: subprocess-exited-with-error × Running setup.py install for lru-dict did not run successfully A:

Building this lru-dict requires some c packages and libraries. Install gcc tools:

sudo apt-get install build-essential

along with python-tools for dev:

sudo apt-get install python3-dev

try them inside container too....this should work

Q: 'CXXABI_1.3.11' not found` A:

Your cross-GCC comes with a version of libstdc++.so which is not compatible with the one installed on your system. You can either run compiled program with modified LD_LIBRARY_PATH (or -Wl,-rpath), pointing to directory with cross-compiler's libstdc++.so, or downgrade your cross-compiler to match your distro.
